prime.problem: A count table tells you how often each pair occurred, but it doesn't produce anything. Without a way to turn counts into choices you can't see what the model learned, and you can't make a single new name.
prime.fits: This card follows the 27×27 count table N. The toolkit card on probability distributions showed how to sample from a list of probabilities; here that one draw goes into a loop that feeds each character back in as the next row to read.
expect: a row of N normalised into probabilities
the sampling loop that stops at '.'
prime.goal: Write the sampling loop from memory, explain why its names are name-ish but still bad, and say why sampling beats both uniform guessing and always picking the most likely character.

attend: Why does the loop start at index 0 and stop when it draws index 0, and what does that one token stand for in each role?
What would happen to every name if you took the argmax of each row instead of drawing from it?
Which part of the bigram setup lets it produce one-letter names that never occur in names.txt?
Why does the same seed give 'mor.' in the video and 'cexze.' on torch 2.14, and what does a seed actually promise?
What does the uniform 1/27 baseline show that the bigram samples alone can't?

must: Divide a row of counts by its total → 27 non-negative numbers that sum to 1 → a distribution over the next character → torch.multinomial picks index j with probability p[j]
Each draw becomes the next row to read → the name is built one character at a time from only the last character → the loop ends when '.' is drawn, so length is decided by the data's ending counts

Only the last character is remembered → the table can't tell a first letter from a fifth → one-letter names (117 in 1,000, while P[.c]·P[c.] summed gives 0.118) and odd strings like 'momasurailezitynn.'

Drawing (not argmax) → rare continuations still happen sometimes → varied names that keep the data's statistics (mean length 6.31 vs real 6.12); argmax collapses to 'a.' every time and uniform to 26-letter noise
elevated: The seed fixes the stream of random numbers for one torch version, not the samples forever → torch 2.14 draws 'c' first where the video drew 'm' → compare your output with your own lab, not with the video
replacement defaults to False → you can't draw more samples than there are categories → Karpathy always passes replacement=True
reference: the video's samples: mor., axx., minaymoryles., kondlaisah., anchshizarie.

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how the bigram table generates a new name, or draw the loop as boxes and arrows with the stop test. Then say in one sentence why the names are still bad.
checklist: normalise the current character's row of N into probabilities
draw the next index with torch.multinomial in proportion to those probabilities
start at '.', feed each draw back in as the next row, stop when '.' is drawn
a seeded generator makes the draws repeatable (for one torch version)
names are poor because only the last character is known; uniform sampling is far worse

retrieve.q: Explain what makes a row of N into something you can sample from, and what property both the counts and the result must have.
answer: divide each count by the row's total
every entry is ≥ 0 and the row sums to 1
each probability is the fraction of times that character followed the current one

retrieve.q: Walk through the loop from an empty name to the first finished sample: which row is read first, what is appended, and when does it end?
answer: ix starts at 0 ('.'), so row 0 (first letters) is read first
multinomial draws an index, and itos[ix] is appended
that index selects the next row
the loop breaks when the drawn index is 0, and the '.' is kept at the end of the string

retrieve.q: You could generate by sampling, by argmax, or uniformly. What does each cost you, and which one shows whether the model learned anything?
answer: argmax is deterministic and collapses to one name ('a.')
uniform ignores the data: about 26 letters per name and some empty names
sampling keeps variety and the data's statistics
comparing sampling with uniform is the check that the table learned something

retrieve.q: Your samples don't match the video even though you used seed 2147483647. Is your code wrong? How would you check?
answer: not necessarily: different torch versions can turn the same seed into different draws
check against deterministic numbers instead: p['a'] = 0.1377 and the rand(3) demo [0.6064, 0.3033, 0.0903]
and check that re-running gives the same names each time

compare.q: At the end of the lecture the same loop samples from a neural net instead of from P. What changes, what stays the same, and why do the samples come out almost identical?
answer: same: start at '.', draw with multinomial, stop at '.', same seed
different: p comes from one_hot(ix) @ W, then exp and normalise, instead of the row P[ix]
the trained net learns roughly the same probabilities as the counts, so the draws mostly land on the same characters
on torch 2.14 only the 2nd name differs (…ityha. vs …itynn.)

compare.q: GPT-2 samples one token at a time too. What does it add to this loop, and what failure of the bigram sampler does more context fix?
answer: it conditions on the whole previous text, not one character
so a first letter and a fifth letter get different distributions, and one-letter names or runaway strings become much rarer
it keeps the core step: turn the model's output into probabilities and draw with multinomial

predict.q: Change the generator to always take the most likely next character (argmax of each row) instead of sampling. Commit: what names does it produce?
predict.answer: Only one name, 'a.', every time. Row '.' peaks at 'a' (0.1377), and row 'a' peaks at '.' (0.196), so the loop stops after one letter. Greedy picking throws away all the variety that sampling gives.

apply.task: Extend the lab: sample 1,000 names from the bigram table with the same seed, strip the final '.', and count (a) how many are exactly a name in names.txt and (b) how many are a single letter. Then do the same with the uniform sampler.
apply.done: Bigram: 105 real names and 117 one-letter names out of 1,000. Uniform: 6 real names, 42 one-letter names and 30 empty names.
apply.hint: Use set(words) for the lookup, and s[:-1] to drop the '.'. Call sample(get_p, 1000) from the Build-it box.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 117 one-letter names, or the argmax result?
What couldn't you explain cleanly about why one '.' both starts and stops the loop?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: row of counts → probabilities, or one-character memory → bad names?
Would you trust a comparison of two models based on five samples? What would you measure instead?
What will you check first when the next card normalises all 27 rows at once?
